title: Sustainer of all

segments.voice: Yesterday, in every heart, and your line: every heart. Did you give one stranger a real hello? The twenty-second ashtpadi named the Master of all beings, then found Him inside each one. Today: who feeds them. Day five hundred twenty-four.

Split a rock in a field, and sometimes there's a tiny creature living inside: a beetle in a damp hollow, a grub, a pale little worm. Nobody brings it groceries. Nobody checks on it. And yet there it is, alive, with what it needs. Guru Arjan, the same Guru who wrote Sukhmani, used exactly that picture in a hymn Sikhs recite every evening. And it's the picture under today's line from the twenty-second ashtpadi. Today: the sustainer of all.
screen: `A CREATURE INSIDE A ROCK.` → `NOBODY BRINGS IT GROCERIES.` → `THE SUSTAINER OF ALL.`

segments.voice: The twenty-second ashtpadi, which began by naming God the Master of all beings, says that God sustains each one of them. The word Sikhs often use for that sustenance is rijak: daily bread, livelihood, what keeps a creature alive. Guru Arjan unfolds the idea in a hymn in raag Gujri that's part of Rehras, the evening prayer. In paraphrase: why, mind, do you scheme and worry, when God Himself is busy caring for you? Even in rocks and stones He made creatures, and set their food before them. Then comes a picture many Sikhs love. A migrating crane flies hundreds of miles, leaving her young behind. Who feeds them? Who teaches them to eat? Have you never thought of that? It's a striking image: the chicks alone, the mother far away, and still they're fed. Now, notice what this teaching isn't. It isn't a promise that no one will ever go hungry, and it isn't permission to stop working. Sikhs are taught kirat karni, honest work, and the whole institution of langar exists because people do go hungry, and Sikhs believe feeding them is God's work done through human hands. The point is about worry. Guru Arjan isn't telling the mind to stop trying. He's telling it to stop scheming and fretting as if everything depended on it alone. The rock creature and the crane's chicks are fed. And often, Sikhs would say, the way God feeds someone is through you.
screen: `RIJAK: WHAT KEEPS A CREATURE ALIVE.` · `IN ROCKS AND STONES, FOOD SET OUT.` · `THE CRANE FLIES; THE CHICKS ARE FED.` · `NOT A REASON TO STOP WORKING.` · then, large: `HE FEEDS ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed a bird or a pet. If you have a pet, give it a little food or fresh water now, slowly, paying attention. If not, put a few crumbs or seeds on a windowsill or balcony. If neither is possible, water a plant. Then sit and breathe. Watch, or picture, the creature receiving it. Notice that for this moment you're part of how it's sustained. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you give. The bell holds the time.
Sustainer of all. Sukhmani says God sustains each creature; Guru Arjan pictures food set out even in rocks, and a crane's chicks fed while she's far away.
Your line: he feeds all. Today, when a money or food worry starts its loop, do one practical thing about it, then let the scheming rest. Day five hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib hear that God sustains every creature, and each evening in Rehras recite Guru Arjan's hymn picturing food set out even for creatures within rocks.

original.note: Gurmukhi: rijak, sustenance or livelihood, from the Persian-Arabic rizq.

trapdoor: what you thought: he feeds all means you'll never go hungry.
what it means: God sustains every creature, so stop scheming and fretting, and keep working honestly, often as God's hands.
what a scholar hears: rijak is a Persian-Arabic loanword in Gurbani, and the rocks-and-crane hymn by Guru Arjan in raag Gujri is part of the evening Rehras.
